name: Dextran filler

lead: Dextran is one of the synthetic polymers listed among dermal filler materials, alongside polylactic acid, polyethylene glycol and others. Dextran-based fillers are injected to fill lines, restore volume or reshape facial contours.
The appearance payoff is the same as for other fillers: smoother folds, fuller cheeks or lips and a more defined facial structure without surgery.

paras: Filler is injected into the skin or just beneath it by a clinician, and the products differ in how long they last and how they are absorbed. Dextran-based products have generally been combined with a carrier gel. Clinicians choose a filler for the area being treated.

Wikipedia lists common filler effects as bruising, redness, pain or itching, with infection, allergic reactions and lumps less common, and rare but serious events including skin necrosis and blindness from embolisation. In the US the FDA regulates fillers as medical devices, and only six are approved.

angle.text: Fillers add volume where the face has lost fullness or where a person wants more projection. Dextran is one of the materials used in this category, which people turn to for contouring without surgery.

lead: Dextran filler refers to dermal filler products whose active material is dextran, a branched polysaccharide. Wikipedia lists dextran among the synthetic polymers used in fillers, alongside polyethylene glycol, poly(lactic acid) and poly(methyl methacrylate).[1]

Fillers are mostly hydrogels, classified as resorbable or non-resorbable polymers, and hyaluronic acid is the most common type.[1] They are injected to add volume and smooth lines, which is how people in appearance communities use them for cheeks, lips, jawline and chin.

Regulation differs by region. In the US the FDA regulates fillers as medical devices and a provider must perform the injection; in the EEA and UK fillers are non-prescription devices that need a CE mark, and more than 140 are sold.[1]
infobox: Medical device (US FDA; CE mark in EEA/UK)

paras: Natural fillers include hyaluronic acid, gelatin, collagen, chitosan and alginate; synthetic fillers include polyethylene glycol, poly(lactic acid), poly(methyl methacrylate), polyacrylamide and dextran.[1]

Common effects are bruising, redness, pain or itching. Less common are infection and allergic reactions that can cause scarring or lumps. Rare but serious events include blindness from embolisation into the eye's arteries and delayed skin necrosis; when vision loss occurs it is usually permanent.[1]
The FDA regulates fillers as medical devices in the US, and only six are approved. In the EEA and UK, fillers need a CE mark, which does not require proof of medical efficacy.[1]
